claims.claim: The strategy's first-class ApplicationSet item explicitly commits that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and teardown remains a manual per-Application operator action, while the PRD's whole purpose is shipping a deletionOrder field (AllAtOnce/Reverse) that automates ordered child deletion; both commitments cannot hold, and note-2 records that this disagreement was noticed at the incident review but deliberately left without an owner ('needs an owner. not deciding here').

The PRD asserts 'No immediate Risks to consider' for deletion ordering, but T-28511 documents a live delete/recreate infinite loop under RollingSync deletion, and note-2's incident runbook now makes 'switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce deletion before deleting any child app by hand' a standing operational rule until a controller fix lands. The plan to ship Reverse (which waits for full deletion of each app, exactly the wait that never completes when a resource is stuck Progressing) is scheduled as if that restriction did not exist.

Note-2's interim restriction — hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists, because every hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave — directly forbids the configuration described in the pilot ticket T-27949, which pilots the source hydrator on a repository whose ApplicationSet uses RollingSync and reports each hydrated-branch commit being picked up as a source change. The restriction was supposed to be carried on T-27949 but the ticket does not carry it.

T-24578's open request for Source Hydrator support on ApplicationSets asks for exactly the combination note-2's interim restriction forbids (hydrator-fed repos driving ApplicationSet sync ordering); its stated motivation, DAG-based destroy ordering of Applications during cluster deprovisioning, also collides with the strategy's commitment that ordered deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented. Nothing on the request acknowledges either constraint.

T-28927 defines the scope for promoting Progressive Sync to Stable, but two standing interim restrictions gate work it does not mention: note-2's ban on progressive sync in hydrator pilot repos until a debounce exists, and the incident runbook's AllAtOnce-only rule for manual child deletion (T-28511). Declaring the feature 'tested and validated with various use cases' while those restrictions stand means the Stable date is not real until the wave-restart debounce and the delete/recreate loop fix land, neither of which is scheduled anywhere in the corpus.

T-26271's CI diff failures and T-28695's controller diff failures are the same underlying mechanism the platform sync call root-caused in note-1: with impersonation enabled, the server-side apply dry-run runs as an identity without patch on cluster-scoped resources. Note-1 records that the root cause was never written on T-26271, so its reporter is still chasing the cluster Secret credential — the connection exists only in the meeting notes, not on the tickets.

Note-1's decision that impersonation stays behind a per-project flag and 'nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed' blocks T-27833's open request, whose proposed remedy for the namespace privilege-escape is precisely the impersonation feature (splitting control-plane vs impersonated-SA resource handling). T-28695 shows the diff story is still unfixed on external clusters (Server-Side Diff ignores destinationServiceAccounts), so the requesting team is waiting on a freeze it shows no sign of knowing about.

T-28695 warns that making Server-Side Diff the default (#24134) will break every external-cluster user unless diff honors destinationServiceAccounts, while note-1's rollout gate makes fixing the diff path the precondition for any impersonation adoption. Two workstreams therefore converge on the same unowned fix: SSD-by-default cannot ship and the impersonation rollout cannot resume until diff impersonates, and no document names an owner for that fix.

RFC-002's push-to-stage mode explicitly relies on 'some external system' to move changes to the deployment branch, T-26443 shows stale-manifest syncs occurring exactly because that external promoter had not yet moved fresh manifests, and note-1 records the promoter is 'still the shell script, nobody owns it' — parked, not assigned. The hydrator program's cross-team dependency on promotion is assumed rather than owned, and there is already a filed defect whose fix path runs through the unowned component.

Note-1 deprioritizes hydrator History & Rollback (T-27327) to next quarter and moves the dev pair to the progressive sync deletion loop, while T-27327 itself records that 'how do rollbacks work' is the first question in hydrator onboarding. The hydrator pilot (T-27949) therefore continues expanding onto repositories with no rollback mechanism for a quarter — a sequencing choice where the rollout workstream outpaces its own safety-net workstream, and the ticket was never updated to say so.

T-28239's fail-fast commit signing design ('refuses to push any commit it cannot locally verify') and T-26443's proposal to block sync until hydration freshness is confirmed both add gating between the hydrator's push and the sync pickup on the same commit-server-to-syncSource path defined in RFC-002; neither ticket cites the other, so two teams are independently designing blocking semantics for the same pipeline stage, and a signing failure under T-28239 would present to users exactly as T-26443's 'sync served old manifests' symptom.
